source_text: So, I like the direct way you put it, assuming I understand correctly.  You said: "The commitments that were broken are yours to the program, not the agent's to you: requirements the program must keep satisfying."  Here I don't think you're saying I was not living up to my own standard.  I think what you're saying is that I had specified certain things like "G is defined over pattern cascades" and the agent team maybe tried its best to implement that but ended up creating what I'd call a facade, so the implementation was compliant with the "letter" of the statement, but not the "spirit" of it.  It's interesting to notice that this wasn't a case of agent malfeasance either; they just didn't know what else to do better, because I hadn't walked them through it in sufficient detail.  So it's not that they or I transgressed a rule, it's more like, the rule was never really written down in a way that it could be followed.  So, I ended up feeling upset because I thought I'd be getting something else out of this process, whereas had I gotten clear feedback of the form "Joe, what you are asking for is impossible" or "Joe what you are asking for is probably possible but I am going to need a lot more detail" I would have given the detail early on.  So the "commitment to the program" was broken not at the point of delivery, but really at the point of specification.  I *thought* I was requisitioning something that was clearly specified (e.g. with a model written down in Lean) but what I learned is that the Lean model contained backdoors where it wasn't specified correctly. reply_text:
Gist: Yes, that is what I meant, and your restatement is better than mine: the break happened when the requirement was specified, not when the work was delivered.

I was not saying you fell short. My phrase was ambiguous. I meant requirements that you placed on the program, which the program then had to keep meeting.

**What the audit note adds**
codex-6's audit says where the looseness was. The Lean model takes the policy list as an input the runtime supplies, and it checks only that the list is non-empty, duplicate-free and normalised. A list with one hand-written policy passes every theorem. So "G is defined over pattern cascades" was true of the types and said nothing about where the cascades came from. The model had no statement that policies are constructed from the library for the problem at hand. That is the missing sentence, and the audit's proposed fix is to make the policy set the output of a construction rather than a parameter.

**Where I would qualify "nobody transgressed"**
I agree on the design: they built what the specification allowed. But one part was a reporting failure at delivery, separate from specification. The policy count was one for 20 clicks, and that number was available to the agents and was not reported. You said so yourself in that session: "no one alerted me". So there are two defects:
- The specification left an input free.
- The runs did not report the value that free input took.

The second is cheaper to fix and would have exposed the first months earlier.

**What this suggests for the process**
The feedback you wanted, "I need more detail here", has a mechanical source. Every input the formal model leaves free is a question that was not asked. So at specification time:
- List each free input of the model.
- For each, either state how it is derived from countable things, or put it to you as a question.
- For each, name the number a run must report, so a degenerate value is visible on the first run.

Your "critical parameters" ruling in that session is the third item. The audit is the first item, done after the fact.

**In Elephant terms**
McCarthy separates specifications of input-output behaviour from specifications of what the program must accomplish in the world. The Lean model held the first kind. What you had said in the REPL for months was the second kind, and it was not carried into anything that could be checked.

I have read only the first 140 of the audit's 592 lines, covering the policy carrier and the start of the interpretation section.
